statements.new_statement_en: The Jewish character of the state should be anchored more firmly in law, even if non-Jewish citizens feel less equal.

split.name_en: Limiting non-Jewish immigration to keep a Jewish majority
split.plus_en: Constitutional limits on entry, residence and status of non-Jews (immigration Basic Laws, narrower Law of Return)
split.minus_en: Fewer legal limits on non-Jewish immigration, residence and family unification
split.statement_en: Israel should restrict immigration of non-Jews to keep a Jewish majority, even if some citizens cannot bring their foreign spouses to live here.

split.name_en: Jewish character versus equality in the Basic Laws
split.plus_en: Stronger legal anchoring of the Jewish identity of the state (Basic Law: State of Israel, loyalty oaths to a Jewish and democratic state, Zionism as a guiding value)
split.minus_en: Repealing the Nation-State Law or giving the Declaration of Independence and its equality clause Basic Law status
split.statement_en: The Jewish character of the state should be anchored more firmly in law, even if non-Jewish citizens feel less equal.

reason: Weight splits into two distinct issues. About 45% (rows 1, 4, 11: Basic Laws on immigration/entry and status, heavily voted) is immigration policy: restricting entry and residence of non-Jews, asylum seekers and family unification to preserve a Jewish majority; Law of Return amendments (rows 9, 10, 15, 16, ~3%) also concern who may immigrate. About 52% (rows 2, 3, 5-8, 12-14) is symbolic-constitutional: Nation-State Law repeal and Declaration of Independence Basic Law (away) versus Basic Law: State of Israel, loyalty oaths and Zionism as a guiding value (toward). Voters (and lists) can differ between the two: support strict immigration limits yet favor an equality clause, or the reverse. The current q4 joins both with 'and' (character and majority), which breaks the one-idea rule; the voter reading it thinks of the Nation-State Law, not immigration. Part 2 keeps q4 almost verbatim (drops 'and its Jewish majority'), same agree key; part 1 is a new statement with the same key direction.
